passage: The school gates opened at 7:45, and Ishita's car always pulled up at 7:40, cool air still on her arms. Today she noticed Pranav coming through the side gate, shirt stuck to his back, shoes grey with dust. "Where do you live?" she asked at the water cooler. "Past the brick kiln. Four kilometres. I walk with my sister." "Every day? Why don't you take a bus?" Pranav shrugged. "No bus goes there." In class, Ishita kept looking at his dusty shoes. Four kilometres. She felt something prickly, a bit like being caught cheating, though she hadn't done anything. At lunch she asked Ms D'Costa, "Why doesn't the bus go to Pranav's side?" Ms D'Costa put down her tiffin. "That's a very good question, Ishita. Let's find out together."

qa.q: How far does Pranav walk to school?
qa.a: Four kilometres, from past the brick kiln.

qa.q: What was the prickly feeling Ishita had in class?
qa.a: It was a kind of guilt, "like being caught cheating", though she hadn't done anything wrong.

qa.q: Ishita chose to ask Ms D'Costa why the bus doesn't go there. Why is that a good next step?
qa.a: It turns her guilty feeling into curiosity about the reason, and an adult can help her understand it instead of her just feeling bad.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt being asked "Why don't you take a bus?"
qa.a: Pranav may have felt a bit awkward explaining, since the answer, no bus goes there, is something he can't change.

grounding: A child who arrives by car notices a classmate walks four kilometres to school, feels uneasy, and starts asking why.

passage: I'm Rukmini, Kamal's didi. Last week Kamal's friend Sonu came over to do homework, and I watched something change in my little brother. Sonu stared at Kamal's desk and lamp for a long time. "You have your own table?" At Sonu's house, he said, there's one room and the TV is always on, so he does sums on the steps outside. Kamal went quiet. After Sonu left, Kamal asked Amma, "Why does Sonu's house only have one room?" Amma tried to explain about rent and jobs. Then I teased, "See, you're lucky," and Kamal got cross. "I didn't do anything wrong!" He stomped off. But that night I saw him clearing half his desk and asking Amma if Sonu could come every Tuesday. I don't know exactly what he was feeling. Something big, for nine.

qa.q: Where does Sonu do his sums at home?
qa.a: On the steps outside, because the TV is always on in the one room.

qa.q: Why might Kamal have got cross when Rukmini said "you're lucky"?
qa.a: He seemed to feel accused, as if having a desk were his fault, so he defended himself: "I didn't do anything wrong!"

qa.q: What did Kamal choose to do that night, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He cleared half his desk and asked if Sonu could come every Tuesday, turning his discomfort into a way to share 🙂

qa.q: How might Sonu feel coming over on Tuesdays?
qa.a: Sonu might enjoy a quiet table for sums and feel welcome, as long as it's offered as friendship rather than pity.

grounding: An older sister watches her little brother notice his friend has no quiet place to study, ask why, get defensive, and then share.

passage:
Monday. Divyansh got 18 out of 20 in the maths test and grinned. Mohit got 17. "I go to tuition three days a week," Divyansh told him. "Don't you?" Mohit shook his head.
Thursday. Buying pencils at the market, Divyansh saw Mohit behind the counter of his father's tea stall, doing homework between customers, the book balanced on a crate. Mohit waved. Divyansh waved back, then felt oddly hot. "Well, I study hard too," he muttered to his mother, though nobody had said he didn't.
Next Monday. At dinner Divyansh asked, "Papa, why does Mohit have to work at the shop?" Papa thought for a while before answering. The next day Divyansh brought his old guidebooks to school and slid them onto Mohit's desk. "I finished these. Want them?"

qa.q: What score did Mohit get in the maths test?
qa.a: Mohit got 17.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh mutter "I study hard too" when nobody had said otherwise?
qa.a: Seeing Mohit working at the stall made him uncomfortable, maybe a little guilty, so he became defensive.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Divyansh, and what did he do with it?
qa.a: Asking Papa why Mohit has to work was the turning point; the next day he offered Mohit his old guidebooks.

qa.q: How might Mohit have taken Divyansh's question about tuition on Monday?
qa.a: Mohit may have felt a little small, since tuition isn't an option for him and his 17 came without it.

grounding: Over a week a child notices a classmate studies at his father's stall without tuition, feels defensive, asks why, and shares.

passage: The results for the regional science prize went up on the noticeboard at the school in Nairobi, and Vera's name was at the top. She was still smiling when Wanjiru said, not unkindly, "Congrats. Must be easier with a tutor and your own laptop, though." Vera's smile snapped off. "I worked for months! I stayed up every night!" "I know," Wanjiru said. "So did I. On the library computer, when it was free." Vera stomped off, furious. That evening, at her desk under the good lamp, she opened her laptop and stared at it. She had worked hard; every night was true. And Wanjiru had worked hard too, with less. Both things sat there together, uncomfortable. She typed, "Sorry I snapped. Want to use my laptop for the next round?", deleted it, then typed it again.

qa.q: Where did Wanjiru work on the project?
qa.a: On the library computer, when it was free.

qa.q: Why did Vera's smile snap off at Wanjiru's remark?
qa.a: She felt her months of hard work were being dismissed, so she felt attacked and defended herself.

qa.q: What would sending the retyped message show about how Vera's thinking changed?
qa.a: It would show she accepts both truths, her hard work and her extra help, and wants to share the advantage rather than deny it.

qa.q: What was it like for Wanjiru to hear "I stayed up every night!"?
qa.a: Wanjiru may have felt unheard, having worked hard too but with far fewer tools, which was the whole point.

grounding: A teenager told she had it easier snaps back that she worked hard, then realises her effort and her advantage are both real.

passage: In the corridor of the coaching centre, the new batch list was taped to the glass. Tanuja had made the top batch. Zeenat, who hadn't, looked at the list for a long time. "Of course. Your dad pays for the extra test series, and you've got a room of your own to study in." Tanuja's ears went hot. "Excuse me? I did four hours every day. I gave up dance for this." "I'm not saying you didn't work." "Then what are you saying?" "That I did four hours too, in a kitchen with my brothers." The bell rang and they walked in apart. All through physics, Tanuja kept hearing it. The test series did help. The quiet room did help. That didn't make her four hours fake. It just meant Zeenat's four hours had cost more.

qa.q: What did Tanuja give up for her studies?
qa.a: She gave up dance.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling and realising all through physics?
qa.a: She felt defensive yet uneasy, realising that the test series and quiet room helped her without cancelling her own four hours a day.

qa.q: What could Tanuja say to Zeenat after class that holds both truths?
qa.a: She could say, "You're right, I had help you didn't, and I also worked hard," and perhaps offer to share the test papers.

qa.q: What was Zeenat trying to get Tanuja to see?
qa.a: Zeenat wasn't denying Tanuja's effort, only pointing out that the same four hours cost more in a crowded kitchen.

grounding: A teenager told she had it easier responds that she worked hard, then sees that effort and unearned advantage can both be true.

passage:
Kavitha,
I've started this letter three times. The first two were angry.
When you said at the bus stop that I only made the state swimming team because Appa pays for the club pool and the coach, I wanted to shout. I've been in that pool at 5 am since I was nine. My shoulders ache every winter. I felt like you'd rubbed all that out in one sentence.
But then I remembered you practising in the river near your grandmother's village in the holidays, because there's no pool near you, and still reaching district level.
So here's what I think now. I did work hard. And I had a pool, a coach and someone to drive me at 5 am. Both are true. One doesn't erase the other, but I shouldn't pretend the second isn't there.
Can we talk tomorrow?
Shalini

qa.q: At what time has Shalini been in the pool since age nine?
qa.a: At 5 am.

qa.q: Why did Shalini's first two letters come out angry?
qa.a: Kavitha's remark made Shalini feel that years of 5 am practice had been rubbed out in one sentence.

qa.q: What changed Shalini's mind, and what did Shalini choose to do?
qa.a: Remembering Kavitha practising in the river helped Shalini see both truths, and Shalini chose to admit the advantage and ask to talk.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel reading "I had a pool, a coach and someone to drive me"?
qa.a: Kavitha would likely feel heard, since the point was never that Shalini was lazy, only that the start was different.

grounding: A teenager who felt attacked on being told they had it easier writes back acknowledging both years of hard work and real unearned advantages.

subtype: Living with a disadvantage others do not see [Receiver]
passage:
Hrithik,
Second semester here. You asked what it's like, honestly, so here it is.
My roommate did a summer coding camp in Class 11. My lab partner's uncle got her an internship with one phone call. When Kartik failed a subject, his parents just paid for a repeat course, no drama. I sit in the library till closing because the hostel room is also where I make calls home and sort out Maa's pension papers online.
Some nights I'm angry. It feels like they started the race fifty metres ahead and nobody even sees the line.
But then I remember: I'm the first from our lane to be here, and I got in with borrowed books and the tuition-sir who taught us free on Sundays. Nobody handed me that.
So, both. Angry and proud. Tell Sir I'm still doing his sums.
Tejas

qa.q: How did Tejas's lab partner get the internship?
qa.a: The lab partner's uncle got her an internship with one phone call.

qa.q: Why does Tejas feel both angry and proud?
qa.a: Angry because classmates started "fifty metres ahead" with help no one sees, and proud because Tejas got in, first from the lane, with borrowed books and free Sunday tuition.

qa.q: What could Tejas do with the anger so it doesn't take over?
qa.a: Tejas could keep naming it honestly, as in this letter, while leaning on the pride and on people like the tuition-sir who backed Tejas.

qa.q: How might the tuition-sir feel hearing "I'm still doing his sums"?
qa.a: The tuition-sir would probably feel proud and moved, seeing those free Sundays carry a student this far.

grounding: A first-generation student sees peers' hidden advantages and feels both resentment at the uneven start and pride in how far they have come.

subtype: Living with a disadvantage others do not see [Receiver]
passage: Aadhya, you asked for the real version for the magazine, so here it is. I'm Yash, final-year commerce, from a government school in a town you've probably never heard of. In first year I thought everyone here was just smarter. Then I noticed things. Friends failing a paper and saying, "No stress, Papa will get me into his friend's firm anyway." People with uncles in accounting checking their assignments. Me? When my phone broke in exam week, I borrowed one for ten days, because a new one meant my sister's fees. Sometimes I sit in placement talks and feel this hot resentment, like the track was marked differently for us. But I also topped accounts last semester. From that town. On a borrowed phone. I'm allowed to be proud of that too, right? Print that part.

qa.q: How long did Yash use a borrowed phone?
qa.a: For ten days, in exam week.

qa.q: What does Yash feel during placement talks?
qa.a: Yash feels a hot resentment, as if the track was marked differently for students without safety nets.

qa.q: Why is Yash asking Aadhya to "print that part"?
qa.a: Yash is choosing to have the pride told alongside the disadvantage, so the story isn't only about what was missing.

qa.q: How might a classmate with an uncle in accounting react reading Yash's interview?
qa.a: They might be surprised or uncomfortable, noticing for the first time the help they took for granted.

grounding: A student from a modest background describes classmates' invisible safety nets, feeling resentment at the uneven start and pride in a hard-won result.

subtype: Living with a disadvantage others do not see [Receiver]
passage: I'm Parveen, and Imran's been in my study group since first year. Last week the others were planning a beach trip: flights, a villa, "just ask your parents". Imran said he had shifts at the call centre that weekend. He always has shifts. He did his whole presentation on a phone because his laptop died and a new one wasn't possible "this month". When our professor praised it in front of the class, Imran smiled, a proper wide smile I've rarely seen. But in the canteen, when Rhea complained her father had "only" given her ten thousand for the trip, Imran's jaw tightened and he went very quiet. I can't know exactly what he feels. I think it's something like pride and something like anger, taking turns.

qa.q: Why did Imran do his whole presentation on a phone?
qa.a: Because his laptop died and a new one wasn't possible that month.

qa.q: What might Imran's tightened jaw in the canteen suggest?
qa.a: It suggests anger or resentment at how easily others get money and trips, though Parveen can't be sure.

qa.q: What could Parveen and the group choose when planning the next outing?
qa.a: They could plan something that doesn't depend on parents' money and check Imran's shifts first, so he isn't always the one saying no.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when the professor praised his presentation?
qa.a: He probably felt proud, shown by the rare wide smile, since he managed it on a phone without the tools others had.

grounding: A classmate watches a student who works shifts see peers' safety nets, showing flashes of both resentment and pride.

passage: Rosa had got her first job at the design studio in Lisbon through her father's old university friend. She knew it; she didn't pretend otherwise. So when the studio opened a paid internship, she didn't just tell her cousin. She printed the notice and pinned it up at the community centre where she volunteered on Saturdays, where Tariq, who drew brilliant storyboards on the backs of receipts, taught kids to draw. "You should apply," she told him. "I'll look over your portfolio if you want." He applied. When her boss asked for her view on the shortlist, she said, "Tariq's work is strongest. My cousin's is fine, but it isn't." Afterwards, over coffee, Tariq told her how hard it was to get past receptionists without a name to drop. She listened and didn't interrupt.

qa.q: How did Rosa get her first job at the studio?
qa.a: Through her father's old university friend.

qa.q: What does Rosa's choice to pin up the notice suggest she believes about her own start?
qa.a: She seems to know her job came through connections and wants people without them to get a fair chance, without feeling ashamed of her own start.

qa.q: Which of Rosa's choices shows fairness most clearly?
qa.a: Telling her boss that Tariq's work is strongest, even over her own cousin's, shows she recommended on merit, not closeness.

qa.q: What might it mean to Tariq that Rosa listened without interrupting?
qa.a: He might feel his struggle getting past receptionists was actually heard, not smoothed over.

grounding: A young professional openly owns her connected start, shares an opening widely, recommends on merit and listens to someone with less.

passage: At the software company's hiring panel, Samir listened to the fifth candidate of the day. Francis stumbled over a few English phrases, apologised, and then solved the system-design problem more cleanly than anyone else. The senior on the panel frowned. "Communication's a bit weak." Samir had gone to an English-medium school, and his parents spoke English at home; he knew how much of his own polish was just that. "His explanation was clear. His accent isn't the job," he said. "I'd score him highest on the problem." They made the offer. That Friday, Samir started a lunch-hour practice group for new joiners who wanted to rehearse client calls, and mostly let them lead. He didn't apologise for his schooling. He just stopped treating it like proof of talent.

qa.q: How did Francis solve the system-design problem?
qa.a: More cleanly than anyone else.

qa.q: How did Samir feel when the senior called Francis's communication weak?
qa.a: He felt uneasy with the judgement, aware that much of his own polish came from an English-medium school and English at home, not from extra talent.

qa.q: Which of Samir's choices use his advantage well, rather than guilt or denial?
qa.a: He spoke up to score Francis on the problem, then started a practice group for new joiners and let them lead.

qa.q: How might Francis experience the job offer and, later, the practice group?
qa.a: Francis might feel judged on real ability for once, and welcomed in a space where rehearsing is normal rather than a sign of weakness.

grounding: A young professional recognises that his language advantage is not talent, and uses his position to judge fairly and help others practise.

passage:
Subject: That fellowship you mentioned
Hi Rehana,
You asked last week how I got into the policy fellowship at twenty-three. I want to answer honestly. My mother worked in the same ministry for twenty years, so I knew what the forms meant, who to ask, and how the interview goes. That's a head start, not a secret talent. I did work for it, but I also know I didn't start where you're starting.
So here's what I can actually offer: last year's interview questions, an hour on Sunday for a mock interview, and an introduction to Dr Menon, who runs the programme. I'll tell her about your field survey work because it's genuinely strong, not because we're friends.
And please tell me what's been hardest for you in applying. I'd like to listen, not just advise.
Jyoti

qa.q: How long did Jyoti's mother work in the ministry?
qa.a: Twenty years.

qa.q: How does Jyoti seem to feel about having a head start?
qa.a: Jyoti seems honest and steady about it, calling it "a head start, not a secret talent", without guilt or denial.

qa.q: Why does it matter that Jyoti will recommend Rehana's work "because it's genuinely strong, not because we're friends"?
qa.a: It keeps the introduction fair and based on the work, so Jyoti's connection opens a door without bending merit.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel being asked what's been hardest?
qa.a: Rehana may feel respected, since the question treats Rehana's experience as worth hearing rather than just handing down advice.

grounding: A young professional names a family head start plainly and shares materials, time and a fair recommendation while offering to listen.

passage: I'm Rekha, Charu's big sister, and I've noticed my sister has started doing a new thing. When she comes home from school, before she even takes off her shoes, she tells us everyone's marks. "Riddhi got 19, Bunty got 15, I got 17. So I'm third." Yesterday she won a medal in the drawing competition and bounced around the house all evening. Today she came home silent. When I asked, she said, "Anaya's drawing got put on the main board. Mine only went on the class board." Same drawing, same medal. She went from the happiest person in the house to someone sitting on the stairs pulling at her socks. I don't know what's going on inside her head. But I don't think it's the drawing she's measuring.

qa.q: What did Charu win yesterday?
qa.a: A medal in the drawing competition.

qa.q: Why might Charu have come home silent today, with the same medal?
qa.a: Seeing Anaya's drawing on the main board made her feel small, as if her worth depended on where she ranked.

qa.q: How could Rekha support Charu on the stairs?
qa.a: Rekha could sit with her and ask what she likes about her own drawing, drawing her attention back from the rankings to the work itself.

qa.q: How might Charu's parents feel hearing everyone's marks before her shoes are even off?
qa.a: They might be amused at first, then worried that Charu measures herself so much against others.

grounding: An older sister watches a child track classmates' marks and prizes, swinging between pride and feeling small depending on her rank.

passage:
Tuesday. The science tests came back. Tejas had 14 out of 20 and immediately craned to see Vinita's paper: 19. His ears went hot. He turned his paper face down and didn't speak at lunch.
Friday. At sports day, Tejas came first in the sack race. He counted: three medals for Vinita last year, one for him now. Still behind, he thought, but he walked a little taller.
The next Wednesday. Instead of only checking Vinita's mark, Tejas asked her how she'd answered the question about plant cells. "I draw it first, then label," she said, showing him. He tried it on the homework and got the diagram right. That evening, though, he still wrote in the back of his notebook: Vinita 19, me 14. He looked at it for a while, then drew a small plant cell next to it.

qa.q: What did Vinita score in the science test?
qa.a: 19 out of 20.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel on Tuesday after seeing Vinita's paper?
qa.a: He felt small and embarrassed, which is why his ears went hot and he turned his paper face down.

qa.q: Which choice on Wednesday turned comparing into something useful?
qa.a: Asking Vinita how she answered the plant-cell question and trying her method, so the comparison helped him learn.

qa.q: How might Vinita see Tejas asking about her method?
qa.a: Vinita might feel pleased and happy to help, unaware that Tejas had been keeping score of her marks.

grounding: Over a week a child ranks himself against a classmate, feeling small or proud, and begins to use the comparison to learn.

passage: Charu, you're upset because Meenu got more stars than you? Sit here with your Rekha nani. When I was ten, I kept a list in my head of every girl in my class: who wrote neater, who sang better, who had shinier shoes. When I came first, I walked home like a queen. When Sudha beat me in sums, I wouldn't eat my dinner. My mother used to say, "Rekha, you are only as happy as your last rank." It was true. Then one day our teacher put my old copy from the start of the year beside my new one. So much better! I hadn't even noticed, because I was only ever looking at Sudha. Looking at others can tell you where you are, beta. Just don't let it tell you who you are.

qa.q: What did young Rekha's teacher put side by side?
qa.a: Rekha's old copy from the start of the year and her new one.

qa.q: What did young Rekha feel when Sudha beat her in sums?
qa.a: She felt so small and upset that she wouldn't eat her dinner.

qa.q: What could Charu try, instead of counting Meenu's stars?
qa.a: Charu could compare today's work with earlier work, as Rekha nani's teacher showed her, to see real progress.

qa.q: How might Rekha nani's mother have felt watching her daughter's moods rise and fall with each rank?
qa.a: She probably worried, which is why she told Rekha she was only as happy as her last rank.

grounding: A grandmother recalls ranking herself against classmates as a child, her self-worth rising and falling with each comparison.

passage: Sunday afternoon in the flat, the pressure cooker hissed in the kitchen, and Ira lay on the sofa in her oldest T-shirt, scrolling. Pema on a beach at sunset. Pema holding a debate trophy. A classmate's perfect cake. Someone's new puppy. Every picture was brighter than Ira's whole week. She looked at her own last post: a blurry photo of rain on the balcony from a month ago. Everyone's going somewhere, she thought, and I'm here with dal. She scrolled faster and felt worse. Then a message popped up from Pema herself: "Trip's been kind of awful tbh 😅 fought with my cousin, got sunburnt, want to come home." Ira read it twice. The sunset photo had gone up two hours ago.

qa.q: What was Ira's own last post?
qa.a: A blurry photo of rain on the balcony from a month ago.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling as she scrolled faster?
qa.a: She felt dull and left behind, as if everyone else was going somewhere while she was stuck at home with dal.

qa.q: After Pema's message, what could Ira choose to do with her scrolling?
qa.a: She could put the phone down, reply kindly to Pema, and remember that the sunset photo hid a bad day.

qa.q: What might Pema's day look like from Pema's side, compared with the photos?
qa.a: For Pema it was a fight, sunburn and missing home; the photo showed only one bright minute.

grounding: A teenager scrolling peers' polished photos feels dull and behind, until a friend's message shows what the highlights left out.

passage:
"Gopika, dinner. Why are you glaring at your phone like it owes you money?" Arnab dropped onto the bed.
"Everyone's life is better than mine. Look. Tanisha's at a music camp. Ritika got a new haircut and looks like a model. Even Mishti won something."
"And you?"
"I did a geography worksheet. Thrilling."
Arnab held out his own phone. "See this photo? Me on the hill at sunrise. Very cool, right?"
"Very cool."
"I'd been awake since three, I was freezing, and I threw up on the bus. I posted the one good second."
Gopika laughed despite herself. "Gross."
"Nobody posts their worksheet days, Gopu. You're putting your whole Tuesday next to their one best minute."
She put the phone face down. "Fine. What's for dinner?"
"Worksheet-level khichdi."
"Perfect."

qa.q: What had Gopika done that day?
qa.a: She did a geography worksheet.

qa.q: Why did Gopika feel her life was worse than everyone else's?
qa.a: Seeing camps, haircuts and prizes made her own worksheet day look dull by comparison.

qa.q: What did Arnab choose to share, and why did it work better than a lecture?
qa.a: He showed his own sunrise photo and told the freezing, sick truth behind it, so Gopika could see the gap herself and laugh 😅

qa.q: How does Arnab seem to see his sister's gloom?
qa.a: He takes it seriously but lightly, using his own story and a joke about khichdi to pull her back rather than scolding.

grounding: A teenager feels behind after scrolling peers' highlights, and her brother shows her the ordinary truth behind his own best photo.

passage: Last winter I had a habit I didn't notice was a habit. Every night in bed, I'd scroll. Dhruv at a coding contest, holding a certificate. Seniors at college fests. Someone from my old school who'd started a baking business at fifteen. I'd lie there with the screen lighting my face until Ma called, "Yogesh, lights off!", and think: I'm sixteen and I've done nothing. Then one day Dhruv came over to study, and I watched him fail the same maths problem four times, groan, and eat half a packet of biscuits. The certificate guy. He was just Dhruv, on a normal Tuesday. It sounds silly, but that's when I got it: I'd been holding my worst nights up against everyone's best photos. I still scroll sometimes. I just remember the biscuits.

qa.q: What was Dhruv holding in the photo?
qa.a: A certificate, at a coding contest.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling while scrolling in bed?
qa.a: Yogesh felt behind and worthless, thinking "I'm sixteen and I've done nothing."

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yogesh?
qa.a: Watching Dhruv fail the same maths problem four times and eat half a packet of biscuits, which showed the ordinary life behind the certificate.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel if he learned Yogesh had envied his certificate photo?
qa.a: Dhruv might be surprised, since on that normal Tuesday he was stuck on the same problem.

grounding: A teenager recalls feeling dull and behind while scrolling peers' achievements, until seeing a friend's ordinary day revealed they were only highlights.

passage: I'm Ujjwal. When our friend Nandita got the summer internship at the research lab, two of my roommates reacted in completely different ways, and I've been watching both since. Kishore stuck her acceptance screenshot on his wall and said, "If she did it from our college, I can." He made a list: two projects, one cold email a week. He's at the library by eight now. Salil went the other way. He kept opening her profile, then his own, then closing both. He told me, "She's just smarter. I'm never getting anything like that." He's stopped going to the coding club. I can't see inside either of them. But Kishore looks at Nandita's news like a map, and Salil looks at it like a verdict.

qa.q: What did Kishore stick on his wall?
qa.a: Nandita's acceptance screenshot.

qa.q: What does Salil's "She's just smarter. I'm never getting anything like that" suggest about his state of mind?
qa.a: He seems envious and hopeless, seeing the goal as out of reach, which drains his effort.

qa.q: What small step might help Salil turn the comparison into something useful?
qa.a: He could ask Nandita how she applied and pick one reachable step, like Kishore's weekly email, so the goal feels possible.

qa.q: How might Nandita feel if she knew how differently her news landed?
qa.a: Nandita might be glad to have inspired Kishore and sorry that Salil felt worse, and might want to share how she did it.

grounding: A roommate watches one friend use a peer's internship as motivation while another sinks into envy, depending on whether the goal feels reachable.

passage:
Monday. Urmila posted that she'd got the summer internship at the design firm. Sumit congratulated her, then lay on his hostel bed for an hour thinking, she's better at everything, why do I even bother. He skipped the evening studio.
Thursday. In the canteen he finally asked, "How did you even get it?" Urmila laughed. "Rejected by six places first. Then I redid my portfolio twice with Ma'am's help." Sumit stared. Six rejections. A portfolio. That was... doable.
Two weeks later. Sumit had booked a slot with the same professor and was redoing his first project at midnight, lamp on, reference sheets everywhere. When a friend asked what had changed, he said, "Nothing. I just found out the ladder has steps."

qa.q: How many places rejected Urmila first?
qa.a: Six places.

qa.q: What was Sumit thinking as he lay on his hostel bed on Monday?
qa.a: He was thinking she's better at everything and wondering why he even bothers, sinking into envy.

qa.q: What turned Sumit's comparison from a weight into a push?
qa.a: Learning her real path, six rejections and a redone portfolio, made the goal feel reachable, so he booked a slot and started working 🙂

qa.q: How might Urmila feel about having been honest in the canteen?

passage: Sit, Bhupen. You've been staring at Arpit's promotion email for ten minutes. Your Sabina ma'am was twenty once, you know. In college, my friend Anjum won a scholarship to study abroad. Two of us heard the news the same day. Rosy said, "If Anjum can, so can I," and started writing to universities that week. It took her two years, but she went. Me? I told myself Anjum was simply brilliant and I was ordinary. I stopped applying for anything. I wasted a whole year feeling small. The difference wasn't talent, Bhupen. Rosy saw a road. I saw a wall. Now go and ask Arpit how he prepared. Then decide which one you're looking at.

qa.q: What did Anjum win?
qa.a: A scholarship to study abroad.

qa.q: How did young Sabina feel after hearing Anjum's news?
qa.a: She felt ordinary and small, telling herself Anjum was simply brilliant, and she stopped applying.

qa.q: What is Sabina ma'am suggesting Bhupen do, and why?
qa.a: To ask Arpit how he prepared, so Bhupen can see a road rather than a wall and choose real steps.

qa.q: How might Rosy have seen Anjum's scholarship?
qa.a: Rosy saw it as proof that it was possible for people like them, which pushed her to start writing to universities.

grounding: An elder recalls how the same friend's success spurred one young woman on and pulled another down, depending on whether the goal felt reachable.

passage: Payal was stuck in a crawling auto in the rain, laptop bag soaked, a rejection email from that morning still open on her phone, when Vandana called. "Payal! I got it! Team lead!" Payal heard herself squeal, "Vandu, you deserve it!" And she meant it. She also felt something sharp and cold under her ribs. They had joined the company in the same month. After the call the auto still hadn't moved, and she let herself sit with it: I'm happy for her. I'm jealous. I'm scared I'm falling behind. All three. That evening she texted: "Honestly? I'm so proud of you, and also a bit jealous, because today was rough for me. But mostly proud. Dinner on me Saturday?" Vandana replied with a row of hearts and: "Thank you for telling me. Dinner on ME."

qa.q: What role did Vandana get?
qa.a: Team lead.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling after the call, stuck in the auto?
qa.a: Happy for Vandana, jealous, and scared of falling behind, all at once.

qa.q: Why did Payal's honest text leave room for real congratulation?
qa.a: By naming the jealousy and her rough day openly, she didn't have to fake anything, so "mostly proud" could be fully true.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt reading "also a bit jealous"?
qa.a: Vandana seems touched rather than hurt, thanking Payal for telling her and insisting on paying for dinner herself.

grounding: On a bad day, a young woman hears of her friend's promotion, feels happy and stung together, and admits both honestly.

subtype: Feeling small at a friend's success [Receiver]
passage: The terrace of Ira's building in Pune was strung with fairy lights, and everyone had phones out when Ira held up her hand and said, "We're engaged!" Aadhya screamed with the rest and hugged her hard. Then she went to refill the lemonade and stood by the water tank for a minute, breathing. Ira was her oldest friend. Ira was happy. And Aadhya felt, very suddenly, like the only one on the terrace still at the starting line. Later, when the others had left, Ira found her washing glasses. "You went quiet." Aadhya put down the glass. "I'm really happy for you. And a small, silly part of me feels left behind. I didn't want to hide it and be weird with you." Ira laughed and hugged her. "You're not behind. You're my maid of honour. Now dry these."

qa.q: Where was the engagement announced?
qa.a: On the terrace of Ira's building in Pune, under fairy lights.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya stand by the water tank for a minute?
qa.a: She needed to steady herself, suddenly feeling like the only one still at the starting line, even while happy for Ira.

qa.q: What did Aadhya choose to do when Ira said "You went quiet", and why did it help?
qa.a: She admitted both the happiness and the left-behind feeling, so she didn't have to act weird and the friendship stayed honest.

qa.q: How might Ira have felt hearing Aadhya's confession?
qa.a: Ira seems relieved and warm, laughing, hugging her, and reassuring her by naming her maid of honour.

grounding: A young woman is happy and stung at her best friend's engagement, and admitting both lets her celebrate genuinely.

passage:
"So? Say something!" Rajni was bouncing on the sofa. "Senior editor, Jas! Me!"
"That's huge. Congratulations," Jasleen said. The smile came out a bit stiff.
Rajni stopped bouncing. "You're doing the polite face."
"I'm not."
"You are. You did it when I got into college before you."
Jasleen let out a breath. "Okay. I'm really happy for you. And I'm also a bit stung. I applied for a senior role in March and didn't get it. That's not your fault."
"Oh, Jas." Rajni pulled her down onto the sofa. "Thank you for telling me instead of going weird for a month."
"I'd have gone weird for a month."
"I know. Now can I be excited?"
Jasleen grinned, properly this time. "Be excited. Senior editor! Where are we celebrating?"

qa.q: What role did Rajni get?
qa.a: Senior editor.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen's smile come out a bit stiff?
qa.a: She was happy but stung, because she had applied for a senior role in March and didn't get it.

qa.q: What choice turned the conversation around?
qa.a: Jasleen admitted both feelings instead of keeping the polite face, and saying it wasn't Rajni's fault let them celebrate honestly.

qa.q: How does Rajni seem to feel about Jasleen's honesty?
qa.a: Rajni seems grateful, preferring to hear it straight rather than have Jasleen go weird for a month.

grounding: A young woman feels both glad and stung at a close friend's promotion, and saying so openly frees her to celebrate properly.

passage: Pradeep, since your podcast is about early careers, here's what changed things for me. Last year I was twenty-four, a junior analyst, and every night I'd scroll through batchmates' updates: promotions, startup funding, conference talks. I'd go to sleep feeling like a failure. So I tried something. I opened my work folder from a year earlier and put it next to this year's. A year ago I couldn't build a basic forecast model without help. Now I train the new joiners on it. That hit me. Then I muted about fifteen accounts that always left me low. Not blocked, just muted. And I picked three people, two seniors and one batchmate, whose work I actually want to learn from, and I ask each of them one question a month. I'm Siddharth, by the way. Twenty-five now, and much calmer.

qa.q: How many accounts did Siddharth mute?
qa.a: About fifteen accounts that always left Siddharth low.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel going to sleep after scrolling, a year ago?
qa.a: Siddharth felt discouraged, like a failure, measured against batchmates' promotions and funding.

qa.q: Which of Siddharth's choices keeps the useful side of comparison?
qa.a: Picking three people to learn from and asking each one question a month keeps comparison about learning, not ranking.

qa.q: How might the batchmate Siddharth chose to learn from feel about the monthly question?
qa.a: They would probably feel respected and pleased, seeing their work valued rather than competed with.

grounding: A young professional describes measuring progress against a past self, muting accounts that drag the mood down and choosing a few peers to learn from.

passage: I'm Pankaj. Hrithik and I joined the architecture firm together two years ago, and until recently he checked everyone's projects like a scoreboard. If someone else got a client presentation, he'd go quiet for a day. Lately he's different. Last week I saw him with two sketchbooks open on his desk: one from his first month, one from now. He was flipping between them and actually smiling. When I asked, he said, "Checking how far I've come, not how far they have." He told me he'd muted a few people online who "make me feel like trash for no reason". And he's started having lunch with Mrs Iyer, the senior who does the best site plans, asking her one thing each time. I can't tell what's going on inside him. He just seems lighter.

qa.q: What two sketchbooks did Hrithik have open?
qa.a: One from his first month and one from now.

qa.q: What might Hrithik's smile over the sketchbooks suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt quietly proud, seeing his own progress instead of measuring himself against others.

qa.q: Why is lunch with Mrs Iyer a better use of comparison than checking the scoreboard?
qa.a: It turns a stronger colleague into a teacher, so Hrithik learns specific skills rather than just feeling behind.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel working beside a lighter Hrithik?
qa.a: Pankaj probably finds him easier to be around, without the quiet days whenever someone else got a presentation.

grounding: A colleague notices a young architect shift to comparing with his own past work, muting draining accounts and learning from one senior.

passage:
January. Ankita scrolled through posts from her old college group late at night: new jobs abroad, a marathon medal, a wedding in the hills. She shut the laptop feeling like she'd wasted a year. Even Jyoti, her closest friend, seemed miles ahead.
February. On a Sunday she opened the note where she'd written her goals a year earlier: "learn the data tools, stop freezing in meetings, cook more at home." She ticked two out of three. Then she muted six accounts that always made her chest tight.
April. Now she meets Jyoti and one colleague for coffee every second Saturday, and they each swap one thing they've learned. Last time Jyoti asked how she'd got so much better at presenting. Ankita laughed. "I compared myself to January me."

qa.q: How many accounts did Ankita mute?
qa.a: Six accounts that always made her chest tight.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel after scrolling in January?
qa.a: She felt discouraged, as if she had wasted a year, with even Jyoti seeming miles ahead.

qa.q: Which of Ankita's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Checking last year's goals showed real progress, two out of three, and the coffee circle turned peers into people to learn from.

qa.q: How might Jyoti see the Saturday coffees?
qa.a: Jyoti seems to value them too, asking Ankita for presenting tips, so the learning runs both ways.

grounding: Over a few months a young professional stops measuring herself against others' highlights, checks her own past goals, mutes draining accounts and learns with a few peers.

passage: Vishal, you've told me three times today that you're bad at maths. Who told you that? Listen to your Rajni dadi. When I was eight, our teacher called me "the slow one". Every day: "Rajni, the slow one, try not to hold us up." So I stopped putting my hand up. Why try, if I was slow? My cousin Gopal was "the clever one". He got the hard sums, and he tried them, and he got better. Then in Class 5 a new teacher came. She gave me a hard sum and said, "You can do this. I've seen you think." I sat with it for an hour. I did it. I wasn't slow, beta. I'd just been told so often that I'd started acting it.

qa.q: What did the first teacher call young Rajni?
qa.a: "The slow one."

qa.q: Why did young Rajni stop putting her hand up?
qa.a: Being called slow every day made her believe it, so trying seemed pointless.

qa.q: What might Vishal choose to do the next time a maths problem feels hard?
qa.a: Vishal could sit with it for a while, as young Rajni did in Class 5, instead of deciding in advance to be bad at maths.

qa.q: How might Gopal's schooling have been shaped by being called "the clever one"?
qa.a: Gopal was given hard sums and expected to try them, so he kept getting better, partly because of that label.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how being called slow made her try less while a cousin called clever took on hard work, until a new teacher believed in her.

passage: The inter-class quiz had ten minutes left, the fan was broken, and the hall was so noisy that Naveen and Suraj had to shout to hear each other. Sir dropped the last and hardest question card on their table. "Naveen, you're my clever boy, you take this one. Suraj, try not to be lazy for once, just hold the pen." Naveen grabbed the card and started working, chewing his lip. Suraj slumped back. He'd heard "lazy" so many times this year that he'd stopped doing homework at all. Why bother? "Suraj, what's seven eights?" Naveen hissed. "Fifty-six," Suraj said at once, surprised at himself. "See? You know stuff," Naveen said. Suraj sat up a little, just a little, and picked up the pen properly.

qa.q: What did Sir tell Suraj to do?
qa.a: "Try not to be lazy for once, just hold the pen."

qa.q: Why had Suraj stopped doing homework at all?
qa.a: He felt discouraged after being called lazy so many times, and had started to believe trying was pointless.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that pulled Suraj back in, and what could Sir learn from it?
qa.a: Naveen asked Suraj a real question and said "You know stuff"; Sir could try giving Suraj a real part instead of a label.

qa.q: How might Naveen be affected by always being called the "clever boy"?
qa.a: It makes him grab hard questions confidently, though it may also put pressure on him to always get them right.

grounding: In a noisy, rushed quiz, a child labelled lazy has stopped trying while his friend labelled clever takes on the hardest question.

passage: In the Andheri flat, the twins had names for everything, and so did the grown-ups. Madhav was "our little scientist". Darshan, nine minutes younger, was "the lazy one", said with a laugh at every family dinner. So when the school science fair came, Madhav signed up for the hardest project, a water filter, and worked on it every evening. Darshan said, "I'll just do a poster," and didn't finish that either. "Typical," Papa said. But Kusum maasi, visiting for the week, noticed something: Darshan fixing the broken doorbell with a screwdriver, carefully, for an hour. "That's not lazy," she told him. "That's an engineer." Darshan stared at her. The next evening he asked Madhav if he could help with the filter's pipes.

qa.q: What did Darshan fix with a screwdriver?
qa.a: The broken doorbell.

qa.q: Why might Darshan have said "I'll just do a poster"?
qa.a: After being called the lazy one at every dinner, he may have felt discouraged and believed hard projects weren't meant for him.

qa.q: Which choice by Kusum maasi changed things for Darshan?
qa.a: She noticed his careful work on the doorbell and named it, "That's an engineer", giving him a new label to live up to.

qa.q: How might Madhav's "little scientist" label have shaped his choices?
qa.a: It gave Madhav the confidence to pick the hardest project and keep at it every evening.

grounding: A child called lazy at home gives up on hard tasks while his twin, called a scientist, takes them on, until an aunt sees him differently.
